title: Biological Control: Predators, Parasitoids & Microbial Agents

content.overview: Biological control uses living organisms or biological agents to suppress pests or pathogens. Success depends on correct target identification, timing, environmental compatibility, release/establishment strategy and avoiding interventions that destroy the beneficial population.

vocabulary.definition: A beneficial organism that consumes multiple prey individuals during its life.
An organism whose immature stage develops on or in a host and ultimately kills it.
Practices that preserve or support existing natural enemies and beneficial organisms.

sections.title: Match the agent to target and life stage
sections.body: Biocontrol agents differ in prey/host range, preferred life stage and environmental requirements. Identification errors or late deployment can reduce performance.

sections.title: Start before populations overwhelm the system
sections.body: University greenhouse guidance emphasizes that many biological controls are most effective when established early, before pest populations become high. Monitoring therefore remains central to successful deployment.

sections.title: Compatibility is part of the control plan
sections.body: Some pesticides, disinfectants or environmental changes can harm beneficial organisms. A biological-control program needs compatibility review before adding another intervention.

workedExamples: Releasing a predator after a pest outbreak has already exceeded the beneficial's suppression capacity is not equivalent to establishing the predator preventively under low pest pressure.
commonMistakes: Assuming all beneficials work against all pest stages.
Ignoring pesticide residual effects on natural enemies.
Treating biological control as a no-monitoring strategy.
content.practicalApplication: For a chosen greenhouse pest, build a biological-control decision table covering target life stage, beneficial candidate, environmental compatibility, release timing, monitoring method and failure/escalation criteria.
content.summary: Biological control is a monitored system, not a one-time product. Target fit, timing and compatibility determine whether beneficials can contribute meaningful suppression.
